subject: math
title: Adding and Subtracting to 10 000
seo_title: Grade 4 Adding and Subtracting to 10 000 Worksheets: Regrouping and Decimals (Ontario)
standard_text: Represent and solve problems involving the addition and subtraction of whole numbers that add up to no more than 10 000 and of decimal tenths, using appropriate tools, strategies, and algorithms
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on adding and subtracting to 10 000 and decimal tenths, matched to the Ontario curriculum: mental math, column addition and subtraction with regrouping, subtracting across zeros and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Line up the places (and the decimal points). Regroup when you need to.
key_sub: Try mental math first: compensate, split or count on. In columns, start on the right; every 0 you regroup across becomes 9. With decimals, 10 tenths make 1 whole, so 4.6 + 2.7 = 7.3.
body_html:
The idea: use place value

Numbers to 10 000 are made of thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Add or subtract the same places. When a place gets 10 or more, regroup: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred, and 10 hundreds make 1 thousand. With decimals, 10 tenths make 1 whole.

First ask: can I do this in my head? If not, use the column method.

Mental math

Split: break both numbers into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Add each place, then put the parts back together.

Compensate

What is 4628 + 2999?

2999 is 1 less than 3000. Add 3000: 4628 + 3000 = 7628. You added 1 too many, so take 1 away: 7627.

Answer: 7627

Count on: when two numbers are close, count up from the smaller one to find the difference.

Column addition

Put ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on. Start on the right. If a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and regroup 1 into the next column.

Estimate first to see if your answer makes sense: 4000 + 2000 = 6000, and 6254 is close.

Column subtraction, including across zeros

Always take the bottom digit from the top digit. If the top digit is smaller, regroup 1 from the next column. If the next column is 0, go left to the first digit that is not 0. Every 0 you pass becomes 9.

Check with the inverse: 3732 + 1268 = 5000. You get back to the start, so the answer is right.

Adding and subtracting decimal tenths

Line up the decimal points, so tenths are under tenths. Then add or subtract just like whole numbers. Put the decimal point in the answer right under the others.

Subtract tenths

What is 6.2 − 3.5?

Tenths: 2 − 5. Regroup 1 whole as 10 tenths: 12 − 5 = 7. Wholes: 5 − 3 = 2. Check: 2.7 + 3.5 = 6.2.

Answer: 2.7

For a whole number, write .0: 8 − 2.7 is 8.0 − 2.7 = 5.3.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Not regrouping (3769 + 2485 = 5144)Write the regrouped 1 under the next column and add it in
Taking the smaller digit from the larger one (7243 − 3586 = 4343)Always take the bottom digit from the top digit. Regroup when the top is smaller
Making each 0 into 10 instead of 9 (5000 − 1268 = 3842)Only the last place gets 10. Each 0 you pass gives 1 away, so it becomes 9
Lining up the numbers on the left (5236 + 471 = 9946)Line up the ones on the right: 5236 + 471 = 5707
Writing 13 tenths as .13 (4.6 + 2.7 = 6.13)10 tenths make 1 whole: 4.6 + 2.7 = 7.3
Not lining up the decimal points (12 + 4.6 = 5.8)Write 12 as 12.0 and line up the points: 12.0 + 4.6 = 16.6

faq.q: What does Grade 4 learn about adding and subtracting in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: Students add and subtract whole numbers that add up to no more than 10 000, and decimal tenths. They use mental math, tools like number lines, and algorithms such as the column method to solve problems.

faq.q: How do you subtract across zeros, like 5000 − 1268?
faq.a: Go left to the first digit that is not 0 and regroup from there; each 0 you pass becomes 9. 5000 becomes 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones, so 5000 − 1268 = 3732.

faq.q: How do you add and subtract decimals in Grade 4?
faq.a: Line up the decimal points and work like whole numbers, remembering that 10 tenths make 1 whole. For example, 4.6 + 2.7 = 7.3, and 8 − 2.7 is worked as 8.0 − 2.7 = 5.3.

faq.q: What mental math strategies help with adding and subtracting big numbers?
faq.a: Compensation (for 4628 + 2999, add 3000 and take 1 away), splitting numbers by place value, and counting on along a number line to find a difference. Estimating first helps catch mistakes.

items.e: Split 0.5 into 0.3 and 0.2. 3.7 + 0.3 = 4. 4 + 0.2 = 4.2. (3.12 comes from writing 7 + 5 = 12 tenths as .12. 12 tenths is 1 whole and 2 tenths.)

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ + 2.5 = 6.1
items.e: Use the inverse: 6.1 − 2.5. Tenths: 1 − 5, so regroup 1 whole as 10 tenths: 11 − 5 = 6. Wholes: 5 − 2 = 3. The box is 3.6. Check: 3.6 + 2.5 = 6.1.

items.q: What is 25.4 + 3.7?
items.e: Line up the decimal points: 25.4 + 3.7. Tenths: 4 + 7 = 11 tenths. Write 1 and regroup 1 whole. Wholes: 25 + 3 + 1 = 29. 25.4 + 3.7 = 29.1. (62.4 comes from lining up 3.7 under 25 as if it were 37.)

sets.title: Word problems: road trips and fundraisers

items.q: The Patel family drove 1786 km on a summer road trip from Toronto to Halifax. On the way home they took a different road and drove 1849 km. How far did they drive altogether?
items.e: Put the two parts of the trip together, so add. 1786 + 1849 = 3635. Check: 3635 − 1849 = 1786.

items.q: Our school’s Terry Fox Run raised $2736. The spring fun fair raised $1895. How much did the two events raise altogether?
A tour bus drove 3678 km in May and 2945 km in June. How far did it drive in the two months?
items.e: Put the two months together, so add. 3678 + 2945 = 6623. Check: 6623 − 2945 = 3678.

items.q: The Nguyen family’s road trip from Toronto to Vancouver is 4420 km long. They have driven 2675 km so far. How many kilometres are left?
items.e: Find the distance left, so subtract. 4420 − 2675 = 1745. Check: 1745 + 2675 = 4420.

items.q: The school council wants to raise $8000 for a new playground. So far it has raised $5347. How much more does it need?
items.e: Find what is still needed, so subtract. $8000 − $5347 = $2653. Check: $2653 + $5347 = $8000.

items.q: The school read-a-thon goal is 10 000 minutes of reading. Students have read 6852 minutes so far. How many more minutes do they need to read?
items.e: Find what is still to come, so subtract. 10 000 − 6852 = 3148. Check: 3148 + 6852 = 10 000.

items.q: A museum in Ottawa had 6214 visitors on Saturday and 3785 visitors on Monday. How many more visitors came on Saturday?
items.e: How many more means find the difference, so subtract. 6214 − 3785 = 2429. Check: 2429 + 3785 = 6214.

items.q: A Grade 4 class had some money in its field trip fund. A bake sale added $1375. Now the fund has $3020. How much was in the fund before the bake sale?
items.e: Work backwards. Take away what was added: $3020 − $1375 = $1645. Check: $1645 + $1375 = $3020.

items.q: A school collected 2465 cans of food for the food bank in October. In November it collected 1758 more cans than in October. How many cans did it collect in the two months?
items.e: Step 1, November’s cans: 2465 + 1758 = 4223. Step 2, both together: 2465 + 4223 = 6688.

items.q: The Okafor family planned a 5000 km road trip around Ontario and Quebec. They drove 1876 km in week 1 and 1659 km in week 2. How many kilometres are left?
items.e: Step 1, kilometres driven: 1876 + 1659 = 3535. Step 2, kilometres left: 5000 − 3535 = 1465.

items.q: A tour bus drove 3426 km on trips to Niagara Falls in June. In July it drove 968 km less. How far did it drive in the two months?
Leah’s family drove 1487 km to get to Thunder Bay, then 869 km on day trips. Benjamin’s family drove 3000 km on their summer holiday. How many more kilometres did Benjamin’s family drive?
items.e: Step 1, Leah’s family: 1487 + 869 = 2356. Step 2, find the difference: 3000 − 2356 = 644.

items.q: The school wants to raise $10 000 for new library books. The fall fun fair raised $3957 and the spring carnival raised $2864. How much more does the school need?
items.e: Step 1, money raised: $3957 + $2864 = $6821. Step 2, money still needed: $10 000 − $6821 = $3179.

items.q: The school had $5436 in its field trip fund. It spent $2867 on buses for a trip to Ottawa. Then a bake sale raised $1385. How much money is in the fund now?
items.e: Step 1, after spending: $5436 − $2867 = $2569. Step 2, after the bake sale: $2569 + $1385 = $3954.

items.q: Ava’s class raised $1268 at a pizza lunch fundraiser. Arjun’s class raised $475 more. How much did the two classes raise altogether?
items.e: Step 1, Arjun’s class: $1268 + $475 = $1743. Step 2, both together: $1268 + $1743 = $3011.

items.q: The Terry Fox Run had 4000 bottles of water. Runners took 1875 bottles in the morning and 1468 at lunch. How many bottles were left?
items.e: Step 1, bottles taken: 1875 + 1468 = 3343. Step 2, bottles left: 4000 − 3343 = 657.

items.q: A food bank in Hamilton had 5073 cans of food. It gave out 2896 cans. Then a school food drive brought in 1749 cans. How many cans does the food bank have now?
items.e: Step 1, after giving out: 5073 − 2896 = 2177. Step 2, after the food drive: 2177 + 1749 = 3926.

items.q: On a canoe trip in Algonquin Park, Aiden’s group paddled 5.8 km in the morning and 3.6 km in the afternoon. How far did they paddle that day?
items.e: Put the morning and the afternoon together, so add. Line up the decimal points. Tenths: 8 + 6 = 14 tenths. 10 tenths make 1 whole, so write 4 and regroup 1 whole. Wholes: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9. 5.8 + 3.6 = 9.4.

items.q: A hiking trail is 12.4 km long. Mei’s family has hiked 7.8 km. How much farther do they have to go?
items.e: Find the distance left, so subtract. Line up the decimal points. Tenths: 4 − 8. Regroup 1 whole as 10 tenths: 14 − 8 = 6. Wholes: 11 − 7 = 4. 12.4 − 7.8 = 4.6. Check: 4.6 + 7.8 = 12.4.

items.q: Zoe bought 2.5 kg of apples and 1.8 kg of pears at the farmers’ market. Her bag can hold 5 kg. How many more kilograms can the bag hold?
items.e: Step 1, the fruit: 2.5 + 1.8 = 4.3 kg (5 + 8 = 13 tenths, so write 3 and regroup 1 whole). Step 2, the space left: write 5 as 5.0. 5.0 − 4.3 = 0.7 kg. Check: 0.7 + 4.3 = 5.0.
